package_info.package_manager: N/A (custom Linux malware, not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (targets multiple outdated WordPress plugins and themes)
package_info.why_malicious: The malware exploits 30 vulnerabilities in outdated WordPress plugins and themes to inject malicious JavaScript into websites, enabling remote command execution and persistent compromise of WordPress-based sites.

execution_context.file_location: Injected into WordPress PHP files or via malicious Linux binary

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malware exploits vulnerabilities in WordPress plugins/themes to inject malicious JavaScript into website pages.
malicious_snippets.code_language: javascript (injected), exploit code likely in C/bash/php
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the malware scans for vulnerable WordPress plugins/themes, exploits them to gain write access, and injects malicious JavaScript into website content, resulting in persistent client-side compromise and potential further payload delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated exploitation of multiple vulnerabilities and injection of unauthorized JavaScript into website content is a hallmark of web compromise and drive-by attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal WordPress operation does not involve arbitrary JavaScript injection via plugin/theme vulnerabilities; legitimate updates would not inject code in this manner.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Website administrators may inject JavaScript for analytics or features, but not via automated exploitation of vulnerabilities.
key_indicators: Automated scanning and exploitation of multiple plugin/theme vulnerabilities
Unauthorized modification of website files to include JavaScript
Persistence across both 32-bit and 64-bit Linux systems

execution_context.file_location: Malicious Linux binary or script running on the server

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malware provides remote command execution capabilities to the attacker after successful exploitation.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after exploiting WordPress vulnerabilities, the malware opens a backdoor that allows the attacker to send remote commands to the compromised server, enabling full control and further malicious activity.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remote command execution backdoors are a primary goal of server malware, enabling attackers to maintain persistence and escalate attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate WordPress or Linux server processes do not open arbitrary remote command channels post-exploitation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools exist, but are installed intentionally and with authentication, not via exploitation.
key_indicators: Backdoor functionality for remote command execution

attack_chain.action: Malware scans for and exploits 30 known vulnerabilities in outdated WordPress plugins and themes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Gains write access to website files and server

attack_chain.action: Malware injects malicious JavaScript into WordPress website content.
attack_chain.leads_to: Client-side compromise and potential further payload delivery

attack_chain.action: Malware establishes a backdoor for remote command execution on the compromised Linux server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent remote access and control

behavioral_signatures: Automated exploitation of multiple WordPress plugin/theme vulnerabilities
Unauthorized injection of JavaScript into website content
Establishment of remote command execution backdoors on Linux servers
file_indicators: Unexpected modifications to WordPress PHP or JavaScript files
Presence of unknown binaries or scripts with network capabilities
Altered plugin/theme files not matching official releases
network_indicators: Outbound connections from web server to attacker-controlled IPs/domains
Unusual command-and-control traffic from Linux server
Unexpected HTTP requests or payloads in website content
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unauthorized changes to WordPress files, especially injected JavaScript. Detect exploitation attempts against known vulnerable plugins/themes. Watch for new or unknown binaries/scripts running on the server with network activity. Analyze outbound network traffic for signs of command-and-control or data exfiltration. Use file integrity monitoring and behavioral EDR solutions to identify post-exploitation backdoor activity.
